BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Near to slightly below normal temperatures will continue as cold air stays firmly in place through the long term period.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued warm and dry conditions Friday.
- Windy conditions this evening with a slight chance of thunderstorms along the front tonight with valley rain and high elevation snow.
- Cooler and unsettled pattern next week with snow levels lowering to valley floors by the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A strong cold front will move across the area this afternoon and evening bringing showers, mountain snow, and a slight chance of thunderstorms along the cold front. Strong prefrontal winds this afternoon, with values up to 50 kts in southern Twin Falls County, where a wind advisory has been issued. These winds will continue through this evening ahead of the cold front. This system will be quick-hitting and weaken as it moves inland, with precipitation ending from the west late Friday night through early Saturday morning. Rain amounts of 0.10-0.25 inch will be common across southeast Oregon and the lower elevations of southwest Idaho, with 0.30-0.60 inch across the mountains. Snow levels will be above 7000 feet initially and only fall to 5500-6500 feet behind the cold front, limiting accumulating snow to higher mountains. Winds will decrease behind the front to 5-15 mph on Saturday, except gusts 15-30 mph will persist in the Magic Valley. Highs Saturday will be 10-15 degrees cooler in most areas, but still several degrees above normal. An upper level ridge will begin building overhead on Saturday as the system moves east with partly to mostly sunny skies. The next system approaches the area on Sunday with showers developing in eastern OR by Sunday morning. The system will be slow to move across eastern OR, reaching southwest Idaho by late Sunday evening into Monday morning. Light precipitation amounts with this system, generally under 0.25 inch.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper level trough will bring another push of cool and wet weather on Monday and Tuesday. Breezy winds, valley rain, and mountain snow will begin late Monday into early Tuesday. Snow levels will start at 5500-6500 feet, dropping to 4500-5500 feet by Tuesday morning. This will bring minor snow accumulation to the Central Idaho Mountains and the Idaho-Nevada border, with Tuesday night snowfall totals between 1 to 3 inches. A ridge of high pressure will briefly build into the region on Wednesday, bringing mostly dry conditions.

Near to slightly below normal temperatures will continue as cold air stays firmly in place through the long term period. Model agreement remains high through Friday with a deeper upper level low bringing much colder air and another hit of precipitation to the region late Wednesday into early Friday. Some model disagreement exists with how low snow levels will drop, with about three quarters of the GFS/ECMWF ensemble solutions favoring snow levels dropping to valley floors by Thursday night. This would bring the first measurable snowfall to the Treasure Valley for the season. Considerable variability exists in the high temperature forecast, with Thursday and Friday highs ranging from the upper 30s to the upper 40s. Current forecast favors the warmer range of these outcomes, with snow levels only dropping to 3000-4000 feet MSL and rain staying the dominant precipitation type for most lower elevation valleys through Friday. Precipitation will linger over the region through Friday morning, tapering off as high pressure begins to build back into the region by the weekend.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A brief period of upper-level ridging is expected to return over the region on Monday that will bring a slight warmup and drier conditions for the first few days of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will prevail today, followed by more seasonable temperatures this weekend into next week.
- Chances for rain and snow showers across the high country Saturday, with a few showers possible over the eastern plains.
- A more active storm track looking likely for next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The persistent upper-level ridge that has been parked over the region, keeping above-normal temperatures and dry conditions in place, is finally beginning to shift eastward today. This will establish a more favorable storm track for approaching systems, essentially opening the door to a more active weather pattern heading into next week.

The first of what looks to be three separate disturbances expected to move across the western CONUS this week can be seen on water vapor imagery as an open trough moving through SoCal and Arizona early this morning. As this approaches, we will see a transition to southerly flow aloft over Colorado as the day progresses. Today's afternoon high temperatures are on track to reach the low to mid 60s across the plains, outside of where morning fog has limited the sun from heating things up so far today. Therefore, areas in our far northeastern corner and Lincoln County will be slightly cooler than our more densely populated areas along the urban corridor, where only some high cirrus are in place. Our mountain valleys should see temperatures warm into the low to mid 50s.

Moisture is expected to increase overnight tonight as the trough nears, bringing an increase to cloud cover as the night progresses. Across the lower elevations, fog is expected to develop late tonight that may make for some hazardous driving conditions through the morning on Saturday, and may lead to some impacts at DIA with decreased arrival and departure rates possible for those with early morning flights. Overnight low temperatures are forecast to drop into the 30s across the plains, 20s for the higher elevations.

Light mountain snow showers are expected to develop through the morning tomorrow, with scattered rain showers forecast to move over the plains for the afternoon and overnight as latest guidance shows the trough closing off and becoming a closed low over southeastern Colorado. Snow amounts are not expected to be very impressive with this first round of moisture, but a few inches (1-3") are expected for elevations above 10,000 feet, with less than an inch forecast for our mountain valleys. Areas over the Palmer Divide and into Lincoln County will cool enough overnight Saturday that we may end up with some flakes falling before sunrise on Sunday, with the best chance for any light accumulations to be over the Palmer Divide. Fog is expected to develop again late Saturday night across Lincoln County before spreading northward across the eastern plains and along the urban corridor, where it will gradually burn off through the morning on Sunday. Outside of the morning fog, quiet weather is expected to return across the forecast area for Sunday afternoon, where temperatures are expected to warm back up into the mid to upper 50s across the urban corridor.

A brief period of upper-level ridging is expected to return over the region on Monday that will bring a slight warmup and drier conditions for the first few days of next week. By midweek, a second disturbance is expected to approach the Intermountain West, though ensemble guidance continues to show considerable spread and little consensus. This is evident in all of the GEFS/AIFS-ENS/AIGEFS spaghetti plots, where 500mb height contours look more like an actual plate of spaghetti than a clear lock on any particular outcome. The same can be said for the third potential disturbance that may arrive by the end of next week. While confidence remains low at this time, this system has the potential to be the most impactful of the three, bringing a more substantial cooldown and perhaps even our first accumulating snowfall across the lower elevations. There is still much to unpack, so stay tuned!

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Friday...For climatology enthusiast, November 20th is the latest first measurable snowfall event in recorded history for Cheyenne, with at least one tenth of an inch of snow measured on the ground.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Chances of precipitation increase over the weekend for the mountains, with a few spotty showers possible mainly along and south of the I-80 corridor.
- A more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: One last mild day is expected today before a cooler and more unsettled pattern takes place this weekend. Latest visible satellite trends are showing fog beginning to erode across portions of the Nebraska Panhandle where weak E or SE upslope flow and effective radiative cooling occurred overnight underneath the ridge. These low clouds managed to hang around a bit longer than expected, so decided to nudge down high temperatures for today mainly along the North Platte River Valley (Scottsbluff - Torington) where fog persisted the longest, delaying surface heating. Expect locations across SE Wyoming to experience another day of temperatures 10-15 degrees above average for this time of year, with clouds increasing throughout the day ahead of our next system. Overnight will be similar to last night, with the potential for fog development mainly after 09Z in the moist SE upslope flow regime. Have the highest confidence of widespread and potentially dense fog along the North Platte River Valley which may extend as far west as I-25. Similar to this morning, wouldn't be surprised to see another Dense Fog Advisory be issued by the overnight shift for numerous counties in the Nebraska Panhandle.

Tomorrow will feature cooler temperatures as the ridge axis translates east of our area with rapidly falling 500 mb heights ahead of a negatively-tilted shortwave trough. As this trough is relatively broad with rather weak flow aloft (15-25 knot 500 mb flow), vorticity and hence differential vorticity advection would primarily stem from curvature vorticity (rather than shear vorticity). We also have to consider any forcing for ascent driven by thermal advection/isentropic lift, which also doesn't look favorable over our area as there is actually isentropic descent (cold advection). So, combining the two, since the base of the trough (and hence curvature vorticity) is progged to be well to our south over Colorado and the main forcing being displaced from our region, precipitation chances look to be spotty at best tomorrow evening and overnight into Sunday. The best chances for any beneficial moisture will be along and south of the I-80 corridor, with the most widespread precipitation south of our area in Colorado. Decided to trim PoPs from NBM guidance for this reason, keeping the highest (30-40%) probabilities hugged against the Colorado border. The Sierra Madre and Snowy Mountains across SE Wyoming may manage to pick up an inch or two of snow, but not expecting anything heavy or widespread at this time.

To end the weekend period, shortwave ridging builds in across the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain West which will bring a slight increase in daytime high temperatures on Sunday and drier conditions. Can expect a decrease in clouds and any lingering precipitation throughout the day, resulting in a beautiful afternoon with highs mainly in the 50s to perhaps 60 degrees in a few locations throughout the Nebraska Panhandle. Dry and quiet weather looks to persist into the beginning of the work week.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Monday...The unusually mild weather continues with broad southwest flow aloft, and high 500 mb heights near 5760 meters overhead. This will induce decent surface lee troughing and mild weather enthusiasts will rejoice with 700 mb temperatures near 6 Celsius and downslope warming boosting maximum temperatures into the mid 50s to mid 60s.

Tuesday...Stronger southwest flow aloft develops across our neck of the woods here in southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska, with a slightly negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft moving across Idaho, Utah and western Wyoming, with surface lee troughing keeping our weather conditions high and dry once again with slightly cooler 700 mb temperatures near 4 Celsius and slightly cooler temperatures for our forecast area, though still on the mild side.

Wednesday...The aforementioned shortwave trough aloft loses amplitude as it moves to eastern Montana and the western Dakotas by sunrise, sending its associated cold front into our counties, Pacific originated. As is typical with these systems, will see scattered to numerous rain and snow showers early in the day west of a Douglas to Laramie line due to dynamics and orographics with some decent snows across our northern Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, though downslope wind east of the mountains and Laramie Range will as usual provide a rain shadow effect with little if any precipitation east of the Interstate 25 corridor and Laramie Range. Orographic snows will continue in the afternoon for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and we may need some type of Winter Weather Highlight such as a Winter Weather Advisory, if model congruency continues.

Thursday...Looks like a windy and relatively mild day for November, the beginning of our typical windy November through March windy season. Strong southwest flow aloft continues, and our wind prone locations such as Arlington, Bordeaux and the Interstate 80 Summit between Laramie and Cheyenne may see some strong winds, and possible wind highlights.

Friday...For climatology enthusiast, November 20th is the latest first measurable snowfall event in recorded history for Cheyenne, with at least one tenth of an inch of snow measured on the ground. Interestingly, this coincides with a decent and progressive neutrally tilted shortwave trough aloft that is progged to move across our forecast area with a rather strong cold frontal passage, which if model timing is correct will produce decent orographic snows for our Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and some likely accumulating snow for lower elevations due to the thickness packing along the front, dynamics and synoptic forcing, especially if the track of the system is a bit further south across Colorado, rather than over Wyoming as currently depicted, so please stay tuned to the latest forecasts from your entire National Weather Service team. In any event. Friday the 20th, will be a cold and blustery day with measurable snow becoming increasingly likely at many locations, although snowfall amounts are quite unpredictable for day 7, one week out. Maximum temperatures will only be in the upper 30s to upper 40s with breezy to windy conditions, only six days before Thanksgiving.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Precipitation lulls beginning Sunday afternoon and through Monday before another wave descends into the western CONUS on Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow returns to the forecast this weekend favoring the southern mountains and adjacent foothills.
- Quiet conditions return briefly Sunday afternoon and Monday before another round of precipitation arrives during the middle of next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Multiple troughs are anticipated to make their way through the Intermountain West over the coming week, bringing snowfall to the mountains and rain showers to valleys. Presently, two troughs are situated to our west, one offshore of the PacNW and one skirting along the southwestern border of the US. The former will carry with it a moderate surge of AR moisture, most of which is expected to get held up on the Sierra Nevada. The latter is delivering its own pool of potent moisture as well. Ensembles are keying in on both sources of moisture transiting the southwestern CONUS and into our CWA, arriving before midnight tonight. As this plume pushes through the warmer valleys, rain showers are expected to develop in the Four Corners region and up towards east-central Utah. By midnight, storms will be climbing into the San Juan mountains where temperatures will be below freezing, hence snow will dominate. Snow levels at the onset of this moisture are hovering around 9000 feet before fropa near sunset drops them another thousand feet and quickly cooling overnight temperatures bring them down to 6000-7000 feet by the end of the event early Sunday morning. The strongest snow rates are expected to hit in the early to middle portion of the event though, likely between 6 AM and noon, and so the bulk of impactful accumulations are likely above 9000 feet. As it stands, above this elevation, accumulations are expected to rest between 4-8 inches in the San Juans (and below 4 inches in the central Colorado mountains and Grand Mesa), though it is worth noting that the NBM 90th percentile is still suggesting that accumulations over a foot in the San Juans at pass level and above are not improbable. Still, given the consistency between forecasts up to this point, we see the likeliest scenario being widespread accumulations under a foot with only localized heavier snowfall exceeding this threshold. Regardless, given the expected snowfall and this possibility of higher accumulations, conditions have warranted a winter weather advisory, which has been issued from midnight tonight through 9 PM Saturday for the southern slopes of the San Juans over 9000 feet. Given the lack of snowfall during overnight periods, it is possible that snow will struggle to stick to roadways, so travel impacts may be somewhat localized throughout the day tomorrow. Regardless, it is imperative to be weather aware and be cautious should you be driving through the mountains tomorrow.

Precipitation lulls beginning Sunday afternoon and through Monday before another wave descends into the western CONUS on Tuesday. Early indications are for similar moisture content to accompany this system, but the overall complexion of the storm is still uncertain. Models are depicting a strong front to accompany the wave, but its passage does not currently align well enough with the heaviest precipitation to support higher snow water ratios. However, given the complex nature of the upper-level pattern at this time, it's uncertain if the timing of the moisture and fropa will hold to this timeline or shift. This would have notable implications on snow accumulations, and so we cannot speculate on that detail either at this time. We are confident that there will be active weather at this time though, so it is safe to plan for potentially impactful precipitation at some point during Tuesday and Wednesday. Furthermore, there is signal of an additional wave moving in quickly behind this one. Additional details on precipitation with that wave will be elaborated on when model guidance becomes clearer.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Thursday and beyond...Models paint a third system to affect the region starting Thursday evening, with some indications that this could be a stronger feature.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - First system to affect the region tonight through Sunday morning, bringing snow to the mountains and showers to the plains.

- Winter Weather Advisory for the eastern San Juan Mts midnight tonight through Saturday evening. Rain/snow mix probable over Monument Hill Saturday evening, switching to all snow overnight with light accumulations possible.
- Another mountain snow event late Tuesday into Wednesday.
- Unsettled weather continues into the next weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Upper disturbance was pushing into southern AZ this afternoon, while across CO abundant high level cloudiness was in place, while low clouds and fog was finally dissipating across the eastern plains. Temps as of noon have warmed into the mid 50s to mid 60s for the plains, and 50s across the high valleys.

Tonight...The upper disturbance to the southwest opens up this evening as it slides east-northeast, becoming intertwined with the longwave trough that extends from British Columbia all the way down into Texas. This will bring snow showers to the Continental Divide starting around 7 or 8 PM, with snow levels between 8500-9000 ft for the sw mts, while the central mts drop from 9k feet to near 7k feet by daybreak. The sw mts are forecast to receive up to an inch of new snow tonight, while the remainder of the mts will likely just see a trace initially. However, snow across the sw mts will continue through the day tomorrow, leading to advisory amounts, so went ahead and issued a Winter Weather Advisory for the eastern San Juan Mts from midnight tonight through 9 PM for 4-8 inches of snow. Across the far eastern plains, there are some hints at low clouds and patchy fog redeveloping late tonight. Forecast grids do not show wide enough coverage to warrant any sort of fog advisory, but following shifts can reassess. Plan on overnight lows around 30F for the high valleys, and mid 30s to mid 40s for the plains.

Saturday and Saturday night...Upper disturbance continues pushing east across New Mexico through the day Saturday, then tries to close off and strengthen briefly over the southeast corner of CO Saturday night. This will lead to snow across the mts, and a rain/snow mix across the high valleys, through the day. Showers will spread across the eastern plains as well during the day, increasing in coverage and intensity through the afternoon and early evening as the system starts to wrap up. By midnight, precip should start coming to an end for the Continental Divide and high valleys, while across the eastern plains cooler air will spread southward on the backside of the system. A rain/snow mix is probably over Monument Hill and northern El Paso County Sat evening, switching over to all snow during the overnight hours. At this time, little accumulation is anticipated. High temps Sat will remain in the 40s for the high valleys, and 40s to lower 50s for the plains. Overnight lows will be in the 20s for the high valleys, and 30s for the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday and Monday...Upper system exits the state Sunday morning, with just some lingering isolated showers across the southeast corner through the morning hours. Temporary ridging then fills in across the region through Monday, with the ridge axis pushing east by Monday afternoon as the next feature approaches from the west. Plan on dry conditions with initially cool temps, moderating on Monday. Highs on Sunday will be in the 40s to around 50F, then climbing into the 50s for the plains on Monday, while the high valleys warm into the 40s to around 50F.

Tuesday and Wednesday...Long range models indicate that another quick-moving system across the area mid-week, with the EC showing a deeper southern track while the operational GFS indicates a more glancing blow. Regardless, the trend is that this feature will bring much stronger southwest winds along with a similar amount of QPF compared to the Friday/Saturday system. This will amount to a period of wind-driven snow, focuses across the southwest mts and which will likely prompt another highlight at some point. Another difference with this system is that it looks like effects will be tied to the higher terrain, while the plains will remain dry. High temps across the plains both days will be in the upper 50s to mid 60s, while the high valleys will warm into the upper 40s to mid 50s on Tue, then just the 40s on Wed.

Thursday and beyond...Models paint a third system to affect the region starting Thursday evening, with some indications that this could be a stronger feature. Forecast snow amounts along the Continental Divide, though far too early, lean towards a significant event. Stay tuned. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The next storm will arrive on Tuesday with colder air associated with it. Median 700 mb temperatures are -8C which could be cold enough to bring snow down to valley floors.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered showers with isolated thunderstorms will develop this afternoon ahead of the main storm that arrives on Saturday.

- Precipitation becomes more widespread overnight with snow levels dropping to ~6500 feet behind a cold front that arrives tomorrow morning bringing a line of heavier precipitation. Mountain snow will be at advisory levels across the southern mountains with lower totals across central and northern Utah.
- Two colder storms arrive next week with the potential for some valley snowfall.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An area of low pressure is moving through southern Arizona and will start to phase into the incoming trough that is moving through the PNW. Moisture from this low pressure system will advect into Utah to produce some low top convection this afternoon. Areas across southern and southwestern Utah will have some increased instability this afternoon along with favorable shear to sustain some weak thunderstorms. Rain rates with these will be on the order of 0.25-0.5" per hour, but they will be moving from south to north fairly quickly so residence time will be short-lived making the threat for flash flooding only a concern for areas that experience any training thunderstorms.

This activity becomes more widespread overnight as the negatively tilted trough approaches. This trough will bring a cold front through the area Saturday morning. Ahead of this front snow levels will be between 8500-9000 feet, but falling to 6000-7000 feet behind the cold front. This cold front will stretch the entire length of the I-15 corridor from southwestern Utah up through the Idaho border between 5-8 am. This front will move through quickly with drier air moving in behind it across southwestern Utah. Central and northern Utah will see a bit more post-frontal moisture as a period of northwest flow helps to keep some terrain enhanced snow ongoing across the central and northern mountains. Additionally, given relatively warm waters across the Great Salt Lake there will be a chance for some lake enhanced snow to the south and east of the lake. Most of this activity will wrap up by late Saturday afternoon/evening.

QPF totals (25th-75th percentile) will range from 0.25-0.75" across valley locations with mountains in the 0.50-1.00" range. Relatively higher totals are expected across the southern mountains (0.75-1.50") where winter weather advisories have been issued for snow totals of 5-10" above 9000 feet. Elsewhere snow totals will generally range from 4-8". Areas that do well in northwest flow could receive more than 12", such as the upper Cottonwoods. If any lake effect snow develops Saturday afternoon then the upper Cottonwoods could get closer to the 90th percentile which would be 15-18".

Some of the coldest temperatures of the season will settle into the area Saturday night into Sunday with most locations approaching or dipping below freezing, aside from lower Washington county. A transient ridge will build into the area for Sunday and Monday, but the short-lived nature will prevent inversion conditions from becoming well established however temperatures will warm back up ~5 degrees above normal.

The next storm will arrive on Tuesday with colder air associated with it. Median 700 mb temperatures are -8C which could be cold enough to bring snow down to valley floors. The latest guidance on this storm exits it a bit more quickly with dry conditions filtering in by Wednesday with some lingering snow across the terrain through Wednesday morning. Another storm arrives by Thursday which will have similarly cold air and even better chances for seeing valley snow totals, but ~50% of the guidance brings the storm further south with the best totals across southern Utah while the other 50% track it from south to north which would bring similar totals areawide.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Avalanche danger will increase throughout the day on Saturday as new snow accumulates. The most dangerous slopes will be shady, high-elevation areas where over a foot of fresh snow forms a slab over an existing weak layer. In these places, you could trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes, at lower elevations, or where you find less than a foot of new snow.

2658.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Danger increases on Saturday as new snowfall lands on weak old snow surfaces. The most dangerous areas will be where winds drift new snow into thicker and stiffer slabs on lee slopes facing northwest to northeast through east. If you find more than 8 inches of drifted snow on steep slopes above treeline, you could trigger a small avalanche that could wipe you off your feet.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes, at lower elevations, or in wind-sheltered terrain.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: A few inches of new snow late on Sturday won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. Most slopes don't have enough snow for avalanches and are safe for travel. At high elevations, steer around isolated spots of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. The weather forecast is calling for 2 to 4 inches of snow, which won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. If you are at high elevations and observe more than about 6 inches of snow with wind drifting, and shooting cracks, steer around steep terrain features at these upper elevations.
